co2.label: normal for open air
co2.note: 451 ppm, which is 0.045% of the air. Outdoor CO₂ is almost the same everywhere (about 0.04%) and does not harm health at this level. It affects breathing only above about 0.5% (5,000 ppm), which happens in closed rooms, not in open air. Near a fire the danger is smoke particles and carbon monoxide.

label: Moderate
headline: The air is acceptable. Safe for most people.
advice: If you have asthma or a heart or lung condition, take it easier outdoors when you notice coughing or shortness of breath.

smoke: If you see or smell smoke, trust that over the number here: the model cannot see a single fire next to you.
Close windows, doors and vents. Set air conditioning to recirculate.
Do not add smoke indoors: no candles, no smoking, no frying, and do not vacuum.
Keep inhalers and other medicines within reach, and drink water.
Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion near a fire can be carbon monoxide poisoning. Get to fresh air and call the emergency number.
If you are told to evacuate, leave early. Do not wait for the smoke to get thick.
indoor: CO₂ builds up indoors, not outdoors. When the outside air is clean, open the windows for 5–10 minutes a few times a day.
Above about 1,000 ppm (0.1%) a room feels stuffy and people get sleepy. A small CO₂ monitor (NDIR type) shows the level.
Fit a carbon monoxide alarm near the bedrooms if you burn gas, wood, diesel or charcoal. CO has no smell and a CO₂ monitor does not detect it.
Never run a generator, grill or car engine indoors or in a garage.
Have heaters, boilers and chimneys checked once a year.

source: Copernicus CAMS air quality model through Open-Meteo. Index: US AQI. Concentrations in µg/m³.
note: From the Copernicus CAMS model through Open-Meteo, on a grid of about 10 km in Europe and 40 km elsewhere. A model, not a sensor.
